theory.intro: The **shortest path** between two vertices in a weighted network has the smallest total weight. Small networks can be solved by **inspection** by comparing direct paths. Larger networks use **Dijkstra's algorithm** to systematically find the minimum weight from the start vertex.
facts: Solving by inspection involves listing all feasible paths between two vertices and comparing their total weights.
In Dijkstra's algorithm, each vertex is given a numerical label representing the minimum cumulative weight from start vertex $S$.
A vertex label is updated whenever a newly checked path from $S$ gives a lower total weight.
The shortest path is found by **backtracking** from destination $F$ along edges where $\text{Label}(V) - \text{Weight}(UV) = \text{Label}(U)$.
The shortest path has the smallest total weight and does not necessarily contain the fewest edges.
The shortest path between two vertices does not necessarily lie within a **minimum spanning tree** of the network.
In practical contexts, the shortest path is not always the best path due to road conditions, tolls, or speed limits.
steps: Set the start vertex label to 0 and record running totals for adjacent vertices
Update vertex labels with the lowest cumulative weight from the start
Trace back from the destination vertex along the minimum running totals to state the path and weight

foundation.question_text:
In applying Dijkstra's algorithm from start vertex $X$, the direct edge $X\text{–}E$ has weight $5$.
However, the running label assigned to vertex $E$ is $4$.
Explain why.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{Label}(E) = \min(5, 4)$
$= 4$
An indirect path from $X$ to $E$ has a lower cumulative weight of $4$ than the direct edge weight of $5$.

Determine the shortest path and distance from Town $A$ to Town $D$.

Shortest directed path: $S\to B\to C\to T$, total weight: $12$

development.question_text:
During Dijkstra's algorithm on an 8-vertex graph from start $S$, vertex $G$ is initially assigned label $19$ via path $S\text{–}B\text{–}G$.
Later, vertex $G$ is updated to label $16$ when vertex $E$ (label $11$) is processed with edge $EG = 5$.
Explain the rule in Dijkstra's algorithm that triggers this update.
development.solution_text:
$\text{Label}(E) + w(EG) = 11+5$
$=16$
$\text{Label}(G) = \min(19, 16)$
$=16$
A vertex label updates when $\text{Label}(U) + w(UV) < \text{Label}(V)$; since $16 < 19$, the label at $G$ is updated to $16$.

$S\to A\to D\to T = 7+8+5$
$=20$
$S\to A\to C\to T = 7+4+11$
$=22$
$S\to A\to C\to D\to T = 7+4+3+5$
$=19$
$S\to B\to C\to D\to T = 9+1+3+5$
$=18$
$S\to B\to C\to T = 9+1+11$
$=21$
Shortest directed path: $S\to B\to C\to D\to T$, total weight: $18$

development.question_text:
The table gives direct travel times in minutes between six Sydney suburbs.
$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{From/To} & \text{Cron} & \text{Hurst} & \text{Syd} & \text{Ryde} & \text{Horn} & \text{Manly} \\ \hline \text{Cron} & - & 25 & 45 & - & - & - \\ \text{Hurst} & 25 & - & 30 & 35 & - & - \\ \text{Syd} & 45 & 30 & - & 25 & 40 & 35 \\ \text{Ryde} & - & 35 & 25 & - & 20 & - \\ \text{Horn} & - & - & 40 & 20 & - & 45 \\ \text{Manly} & - & - & 35 & - & 45 & - \end{array}$
Determine the shortest travel time and route between Cronulla (Cron) and Hornsby (Horn).
Explain two practical circumstances where the shortest distance path in a road network is not necessarily the best path to choose.
development.solution_text:
$\text{Travel time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$
A shorter route with lower speed limits or congestion may take more time than a highway route.
A shorter route may also incur toll costs or hazardous road conditions such as steep, narrow passes.
